parts.text: Many good morrows to your Majesty!
Is it good morrow, lords?
’Tis one o’clock, and past.
Why then, good morrow to you all, my lords.
Have you read o’er the letters that I sent you?
We have, my liege.
Then you perceive the body of our kingdom
How foul it is, what rank diseases grow,
And with what danger, near the heart of it.
It is but as a body yet distemper’d,
Which to his former strength may be restored
With good advice and little medicine.
My Lord Northumberland will soon be cool’d.
Good morning, your Majesty. A very good morning to you.
Is it morning already, my lords?
It's past one o'clock.
Well then, good morning to you all, my lords.
Have you read through the letters I sent you?
We have, my lord.
Then you can see how sick this kingdom is.
How rotten the whole body has become, what diseases are spreading through it.
And how dangerously close they are to the heart.
It's a body that's only a little out of sorts, so far.
It can get its old strength back.
Good advice and a little medicine will do it.
Lord Northumberland will cool down soon enough.
A very good morning to your Majesty!
Is it morning, my lords?
It's one o'clock, and past.
Well then, good morning to you all, my lords.
Have you read through the letters I sent you?
We have, my lord.
Then you can see how sick the body of our kingdom is.
What foul diseases are growing in it,
and how dangerously close they are to its heart.
It's only a body that's out of sorts for now.
It can be brought back to its old strength
with good advice and a little medicine.
My Lord Northumberland will soon cool down.
Sing, boy. My spirit grows heavy in love.
And that’s great marvel, loving a light wench.
I say, sing.
Forbear till this company be past.
Enter Costard the Clown, Dull the Constable and Jaquenetta a Wench.
Sir, the Duke’s pleasure is that you keep Costard safe; and you must
suffer him to take no delight, nor no penance, but he must fast three
days a week. For this damsel, I must keep her at the park. She is
allowed for the dey-woman. Fare you well.
Sing, boy. Love is making my spirit heavy.
That's a real wonder, sir, when the girl you love is so light.
I said, sing.
Wait till these people have gone by.
Enter Costard the clown, Dull the constable, and Jaquenetta, a country girl.
Sir, it's the Duke's wish that you keep Costard locked up.
You're not to let him have any fun, and no penance either. He just has to fast three days a week.
As for this young woman, I'm to keep her here in the park.
She's been taken on as the dairymaid. Good day to you.
Sing, boy.
Love is making my heart heavy.
Now that's amazing, sir.
Heavy, over a girl who's that light.
I said, sing.
Wait till these people have gone by.
Costard the clown, Dull the constable and Jaquenetta, a country girl, come in.
Sir, it's the Duke's wish that you keep Costard locked up safe.
You're not to let him have any fun, and no penance either.
But he has to fast three days a week.
As for this young lady, I'm to keep her here at the park.
She's been taken on as the dairy-maid.
Goodbye to you.
Tonight, say I.
Come, come, it may not be. I wonder much,
Being men of such great leading as you are,
That you foresee not what impediments
Drag back our expedition. Certain horse
Of my cousin Vernon’s are not yet come up.
Your uncle Worcester’s horse came but today,
And now their pride and mettle is asleep,
Their courage with hard labour tame and dull,
That not a horse is half the half himself.
Tonight, I say.
Come on, come on, it can't be done.
I'm amazed that men who lead armies, like you,
can't see what's holding our attack back.
Some of my cousin Vernon's cavalry still haven't arrived.
Your uncle Worcester's cavalry only got here today.
Their spirit and fire have gone to sleep.
Hard riding has worn their courage down, made it tame and dull.
There isn't a horse out there that's even half of half itself.
Tonight. I say tonight.
Come on, come on. It can't be done.
Honestly, I'm amazed. Men who've led as many armies as you have,
and you can't see what's holding us back?
Some of my cousin Vernon's cavalry still haven't arrived.
Your uncle Worcester's horses only got here today.
All their fire and spirit is gone.
They're worn out from the march, tame and sluggish.
There isn't a horse out there that's half of half what it should be.
She is,
When once she is my wife.
That “once”, I see by your good father’s speed,
Will come on very slowly. I am sorry,
Most sorry, you have broken from his liking,
Where you were tied in duty; and as sorry
Your choice is not so rich in worth as beauty,
That you might well enjoy her.
Dear, look up:
Though Fortune, visible an enemy,
Should chase us with my father, power no jot
Hath she to change our loves. Beseech you, sir,
Remember since you ow’d no more to time
Than I do now: with thought of such affections,
Step forth mine advocate. At your request
My father will grant precious things as trifles.
She will be.
Once she's my wife.
That "once" is going to take a long time coming, judging by how fast your father's chasing you.
I'm sorry. Truly sorry that you've lost his good will, when you owed him your obedience.
And just as sorry that she isn't as well born as she is beautiful.
Then you'd be free to have her.
To Perdita
My love, lift your head.
Even if Fortune turns openly against us and hunts us down along with my father,
she has no power at all to change how we love each other.
To Leontes
Sir, I'm begging you.
Remember when you were no older than I am now, and in love like this.
Remember how that felt, and speak up for me.
If you ask him, my father will give up even what he values most as if it were nothing.
She will be, once she's my wife.
That "once," judging by how fast your good father is coming, will be a long time arriving.
I'm sorry, truly sorry, that you've lost his favour, when duty bound you to keep it.
And I'm just as sorry that the girl you've chosen isn't as rich in rank as she is in beauty.
Then you could marry her and be happy.
Darling, look up.
Even if Fortune turns openly against us and hunts us down along with my father,
she hasn't the slightest power to change our love.
I beg you, sir, remember when you were no older than I am now.
Remember how you loved back then, and speak up for me.
If you ask him, my father will give up precious things as if they were nothing.
Is not this buckled well?
Rarely, rarely.
He that unbuckles this, till we do please
To daff’t for our repose, shall hear a storm.
Thou fumblest, Eros, and my queen’s a squire
More tight at this than thou. Dispatch. O love,
That thou couldst see my wars today, and knew’st
The royal occupation, thou shouldst see
A workman in’t.
Enter an Officer, armed.
Good morrow to thee. Welcome.
Thou look’st like him that knows a warlike charge.
To business that we love we rise betime
And go to’t with delight.
Isn't this buckled on well?
Beautifully, beautifully.
Anyone who unbuckles this before we choose to take it off and rest will face a storm.
You're fumbling, Eros. My queen makes a better squire at this than you do.
Hurry up.
Oh, my love, if only you could watch me fight today, and knew this royal trade.
You'd see a real craftsman at work.
An Officer enters, in armour.
Good morning to you. Welcome.
You look like a man who knows how to lead a charge.
When it's work we love, we get up early and go to it gladly.
Isn't this buckled well?
Perfectly. Perfectly.
Anyone who tries to unbuckle this before I choose to take it off and rest is in for a storm.
You're fumbling, Eros. My queen makes a better squire than you.
Hurry up.
Oh, my love, I wish you could see me fight today.
If you understood the soldier's trade, you'd see a real craftsman at work.
An Officer enters, in armour.
Good morning to you. Welcome.
You look like a man with a battle to lead.
When it's work we love, we get up early and go to it gladly.
Before me, she’s a good wench.
She’s a beagle true bred, and one that adores me. What o’ that?
I was adored once too.
Let’s to bed, knight. Thou hadst need send for more money.
If I cannot recover your niece, I am a foul way out.
Send for money, knight; if thou hast her not i’ th’ end, call me cut.
If I do not, never trust me, take it how you will.
Upon my soul, she's a good girl.
She's a pure-bred little beagle, and she adores me.
So what of it?
I was adored once too.
Let's go to bed, knight.
You'd better send home for more money.
If I can't win your niece, I'll be terribly out of pocket.
Send for money, knight.
If you haven't got her in the end, call me a broken-down old cart-horse.
If I don't, never trust me again, take that however you like.
I swear, she's a great girl.
She's a pure-bred little beagle, and she adores me.
So what?
Someone adored me once too.
Come on, knight, let's go to bed.
You'd better send home for more money.
If I don't win your niece, I'm badly out of pocket.
Send for the money, knight.
If she's not yours in the end, you can call me a broken-down old nag.
If I don't, never trust me again.
Take that however you like.
’Tis Gaultree Forest, an ’t shall please your Grace.
Here stand, my lords, and send discoverers forth
To know the numbers of our enemies.
We have sent forth already.
’Tis well done.
My friends and brethren in these great affairs,
I must acquaint you that I have received
New-dated letters from Northumberland,
Their cold intent, tenor, and substance, thus:
Here doth he wish his person, with such powers
As might hold sortance with his quality,
The which he could not levy; whereupon
He is retired, to ripe his growing fortunes,
To Scotland, and concludes in hearty prayers
That your attempts may overlive the hazard
And fearful meeting of their opposite.
This is Gaultree Forest, your Grace.
We'll halt here, my lords.
Send scouts ahead to find out how many of them there are.
We've sent them already.
Good.
My friends, my brothers in this great cause, there's something I have to tell you.
I've had fresh letters from Northumberland.
They're cold. Here's the gist of them.
He says he wishes he were here, with an army worthy of his rank.
But he couldn't raise one.
So he's gone off to Scotland, to wait until his fortunes grow.
And he ends by praying, very warmly, that you come through the danger
and that terrible clash with the enemy alive.
It's Gaultree Forest, if it please your Grace.
Stop here, my lords.
Send scouts out to find how many enemies we're facing.
We've sent them already.
Well done.
My friends, my brothers in this great cause, there's something I have to tell you.
I've had fresh letters from Northumberland.
Their meaning is cold, and here's the gist of it.
He wishes he were here himself, with an army worthy of his rank.
But he couldn't raise one.
So he's withdrawn to Scotland, to wait until his fortunes grow.
And he ends with heartfelt prayers that our efforts will survive the danger and the fearful clash with the other side.
